title: Work that runs without you
desc: What a Cowork item is, where its result lands, and how it differs from a chat.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can describe the full life of a Cowork item — from the sentence you type to the notification that reports back — and say which jobs belong in Cowork rather than in chat.

steps.title: Ask it here, or hand it over
steps.bodyMd:
At Van Dijk Groep, buyer Bart starts every morning the same way: he opens a chat and retypes the same request — *what came in from suppliers overnight, and what needs an answer today?*

Bee Flow has two halves for that.

- **Chat** answers you here, while you wait. You are present, so you can ask a follow-up.
- **Cowork** takes the job away and runs it unattended — now, at a moment you pick, or every weekday — and reports back when it is done.

The page says it plainly: **What can Bee Flow take off your plate?** *Describe it once. It runs on its own — now, later, or every week.*

We follow one job the whole way: Bart's sentence, the run at 07:30, and the result waiting in his notifications.

steps.title: Cowork lives under New Chat
steps.body: The badge on this row counts the items that are still switched on — the ones with a run still ahead of them. Open it and the page splits: your list on the left, one item on the right, and a New task button that clears the selection so you can write the next one.

steps.title: One box, three chips
steps.body: Type the work here; the box says "Describe the work — Bee Flow runs it and reports back". Under it sit three chips showing their current answer, not their name: when it runs (Now), whether it repeats (Once), and who does the work (No agent) — that last chip appears only when you have agents. Send reads Run when the work starts now, Schedule when it starts later.

steps.title: Your sentence becomes the assignment
There is no preview — so check the item
steps.bodyMd:
Reading your sentence and storing the item happen in the same press of the button. There is no step in between that shows you a draft first.

That makes the item itself the first place you see what Bee Flow understood. Open it, read the title and the *What it does* instruction, and correct anything the model misheard under **Edit**.

And if the model cannot be reached at all, nothing is lost: Bee Flow falls back to your own sentence as the instruction, and to whatever the chips already say.

steps.question: Bart's supplier digest runs at 07:30 while he is driving to a site visit. Where does the result end up?

choices.label: In his notifications, under the Cowork category — and every attempt is kept in the item's own What happened history.
In a chat thread he has to leave open, which is why he should not close the app overnight.
choices.feedback: Nothing needs to stay open. A cowork item runs unattended on Bee Flow's side; the result is delivered to your notifications and stored on the item.

choices.label: In an email to him and to the purchasing team.
choices.feedback: Nothing is delivered by mail and nothing goes to a colleague. Notifications and the item's own run history are where the output lives.

steps.explanation: Notifications are the delivery channel: a finished run arrives with the item's title and the full result, with a button to open that result in chat. The item's What happened card keeps every attempt.

steps.title: The chips are decisions; the brief is context
steps.bodyMd:
- **When** — *Run now*, *In an hour*, *Tonight* (18:00), *Tomorrow morning* (09:00), *Next Monday* (09:00), or *Pick a moment…* with your own date and time.
- **Repeat** — *Once*, *Every hour*, *Every day*, *Every weekday*, *Every week*, and on up to *Every year*. A repeat keeps running until you pause it.
- **Run as** — hands the job to one of your agents, which brings its own skills, knowledge and connected apps. This chip only appears when you have agents to pick from; the next card follows what it changes.

The rule that settles every argument: **a chip you touch always wins**. Write "every Friday" in the brief but leave Repeat on *Once*, and it runs once. The model only fills in the chips you left alone.

steps.title: Run as: handing the job to an agent
steps.bodyMd:
The third chip answers one question, and its sheet asks it out loud: **Who does the work?** Underneath, the one-line explanation — *An agent brings its own skills, knowledge and connected apps.* The first row is **No agent**, hinted *Runs as a plain prompt*.

Pick one of your agents and three things change at once.

- The brief runs **as that agent**: its own instructions, its skills, its knowledge bases and the apps it is connected to all come along for the run.
- The result lands in **that agent's chat thread** as well as in your notifications — so you can open the thread and carry on talking about what came out.
- The model tier stops being yours to set. An agent-linked run uses the agent's own model, so the item's tier pill reads **Auto**.

The chip is only on screen when you actually have agents to pick from; with none, there is nothing to choose and the composer shows just the two chips. (Start in an agent's chat and flip to Cowork, and that agent is pre-selected for you.)

steps.question: Bart hands his 07:30 supplier digest to his purchasing agent with the **Run as** chip. What does that change about the run?

choices.label: It runs with that agent's instructions, skills, knowledge and connected apps; the result lands in the agent's chat thread as well as in his notifications; and the model tier reads Auto, because the agent's own model does the work.
Only the name on the row changes. The work itself is identical, and he still sets the model tier for it himself.
choices.feedback: Both halves are off. The agent brings its own skills, knowledge bases and connected apps to the run, and the tier is no longer his to set — an agent-linked run uses the agent's own model, so the item shows Auto.

choices.label: The result now goes only to the agent's chat thread, so the Cowork notification is skipped.
choices.feedback: Nothing is skipped. An agent-linked run is delivered to your notifications in the usual way and additionally writes the result into that agent's chat thread.

steps.explanation: Run as is a handover, not a label: the agent's own setup does the work, its thread keeps a copy of the result, and the tier is forced to Auto. Without agents to pick from, the chip does not appear at all.

steps.title: Chat, or hand it over?
steps.instruction: Four jobs from Van Dijk Groep. Match each one to where it belongs.

pairs.left: Bart needs our payment terms with one specific supplier right now — and may want to dig further.
pairs.note: You are present and you want a conversation. A cowork run never asks you a question back, so anything that needs a follow-up belongs in chat.

pairs.left: A one-off comparison of three steel-frame suppliers, ready to read after this afternoon's site visit.
pairs.right: Cowork — When: Run now, Repeat: Once
pairs.note: Real work, no repeat, and he is not going to sit and watch it. Press Run; the result is in his notifications when he gets back.

pairs.left: Every working day at 07:30, a digest of the new supplier mail with order number, amount and deadline.
pairs.note: Mon–Fri work that must happen whether or not he opens Bee Flow. The row will read "Every weekday 07:30".

pairs.left: Saskia in the office writes a short progress report on the first of every month, from last month's meeting notes.
pairs.note: Same shape, slower drum. She sets Repeat to Every month and picks the moment herself, so the model does not have to guess.

steps.title: Your turn: walk the life of one delegation
steps.instruction: Pick one job you would genuinely hand over — yours, or Bart's supplier digest. In four to six sentences, walk it from beginning to end: the sentence you type, which button you press and why (**Run** or **Schedule**), what Bee Flow derives from that sentence, and where you read the result once it has run. Write it for a colleague who has never opened Cowork.
steps.placeholder: e.g. I type "Every Friday at 16:00, list this week's quotes that have had no reply, with customer, amount and how many days it has been quiet." Because it starts later, the button reads Schedule…

steps.title: What the item tells you afterwards
steps.bodyMd:
Click a row in the list and the right pane shows the whole life of that job.

- **The assignment** — the instruction exactly as it runs, with pills for the cadence (*Every weekday 07:30*), the next run (*next Tomorrow at 07:30*), the agent if there is one, and the model tier — how heavy a model the work gets.
- **What happened** — one row per attempt, newest first: time, duration and the first line of the outcome. Expand a row for the full result, and for whether it was *Started by you* or *Started on schedule*.

Before the first run that history reads: *This hasn't run yet. The history fills in after the first run.*

steps.title: Why Runs and Succeeded disagree
steps.bodyMd:
Between the assignment and the history sit three small cards: **Runs**, **Succeeded** and **Average**.

Runs is the lifetime tally. The other two are counted from the run rows that are still kept, and those are kept for 90 days.

So a large Runs number can sit beside a smaller Succeeded one, and nothing is broken. Once nothing at all is left inside that window, Succeeded reads 0 with the note *older runs are no longer kept* — the honest answer, rather than a comforting *nothing went wrong*.

steps.question: Saskia's monthly progress report touches personnel data. Who else at Van Dijk Groep can open that cowork item and read its runs?

choices.label: Nobody. A cowork item belongs to the person who created it, and there is no shared or organisation-wide list.
Everyone in the organisation — the Cowork list is a workspace list, like a shared calendar.
choices.feedback: It is not shared at all. Every read is scoped to the signed-in user, and opening someone else's item is refused as Forbidden.

choices.label: Organisation admins, from a central overview of everyone's scheduled work.
choices.feedback: That overview does not exist. There is no organisation-wide cowork view; ownership is the only key to an item.

steps.explanation: Cowork is strictly per person: your items, your runs, your notifications. A colleague who wants the same digest types the same sentence into their own Cowork.

steps.title: Apps it may use
steps.bodyMd:
Beside the chips sits an **Apps** button, and the same picker comes back under **Edit** as **Apps it may use**, with a counter reading *{count} of {total} enabled*.

A new item carries no list of its own: it simply follows the apps you have switched on workspace-wide. The hint says so — *Following your workspace-wide list. Switch anything here and this cowork keeps its own list from then on.*

That last clause is the whole trap. The moment you switch one app off, the item has its **own** list, and later changes to your workspace list no longer reach it. The hint changes to *Only these apps are available to this cowork when it runs, whatever you have switched on elsewhere.* The link **Follow my workspace list** hands it back.

An empty list is a real answer too: this one may use nothing. And once an item carries its own list, the assignment shows a pill counting them — *2 apps*.

steps.question: Saskia's monthly report should only touch her meeting notes, so in that item's Apps picker she switches the other apps off. Weeks later a new app is connected for the whole workspace. Does her cowork item get it?

choices.label: No. Switching an app off gave the item its own list, and from then on it ignores workspace-wide changes — until she clicks Follow my workspace list.
Yes. The per-item picker only changes what she sees on screen; at run time the workspace-wide list is what applies.
choices.feedback: It is the other way round. Once the item has its own list, only those apps are available to it when it runs, whatever you have switched on elsewhere.

choices.label: Yes, because a per-item list only holds for the next run and then falls back to the workspace list.
choices.feedback: The list is stored on the item and keeps applying to every run. Nothing expires it; the Follow my workspace list link is what gives it back.

steps.explanation: An item is in one of two states: no list of its own, so it follows your workspace-wide list, or its own list, which wins over anything you change elsewhere. Touching the picker moves it from the first state to the second; Follow my workspace list moves it back.

steps.title: You stay in charge of it
steps.bodyMd:
Four controls sit above the assignment.

- **Run now** — fires immediately without disturbing the series; the next scheduled moment stays where it was. It is greyed out while a run is still open.
- **Pause / Resume** — the reversible way to stop a repeat. The row then reads *Paused*.
- **Edit** — rewrite **Name**, **What it does**, the **Next run** date, the **At** time, the **Repeat**, and which apps the item may use.
- **Delete** — removes the item *and* its history, and that cannot be undone. If there is any chance you want it back, pause it instead.

One ceiling to remember: 10 cowork items per person. Past that, the page asks you to delete or finish one to make room.

steps.question: Bart sent that one-off supplier comparison with **When: Run now** and **Repeat: Once**, and it ran that afternoon. A week later the item reads **Finished** and has not run again. Did something go wrong?

choices.label: Nothing went wrong: Now plus Once means exactly one run, after which the item switches itself off. Finished is the normal end state.
It failed quietly — Finished is what an item says when its run produced no usable output.
choices.feedback: Those are different words. A run with no text shows as "Nothing to report" in What happened, and a real failure turns the item's status into Failed with an urgent notification.

choices.label: It was switched off automatically after its history reached the 90-day limit.
choices.feedback: Nothing is switched off by age. Ninety days is only how long the individual run rows are kept in What happened; the item itself and its lifetime Runs count stay.

steps.explanation: Once is a decision, not an oversight. If Bart wants that comparison every week, he opens Edit and sets Repeat to Every week — the series then starts at the next occurrence.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- **Tell the two halves apart.** If you want the answer in front of you and may ask a follow-up, chat. If the work should happen while you are elsewhere, hand it to Cowork.
- **Predict what your sentence will do.** Bee Flow derives a title, an instruction and a schedule from it — and any chip you set yourself wins over what the sentence says.
- **Know where to read it.** The assignment says what runs, the pills say when, What happened keeps every attempt with its full result — and the finished result reaches you in your notifications (and in the agent's chat thread, if you handed the job to an agent).

Next chapter: writing a brief nobody has to clarify — because when it runs, nobody will be there to ask.

ex-cowork-basics-life.title: The life of a cowork item
ex-cowork-basics-life.task: The learner picks one job to delegate and describes it end to end in four to six sentences: the sentence they type, whether they press Run or Schedule and why, what Bee Flow derives from that sentence, and where the result is read afterwards.
criteria: Names a concrete job with a timing decision (now, a moment, or a repeat) rather than a vague wish.
Uses the correct send button for that timing: Run when it starts now, Schedule when it starts later.
Shows that Bee Flow derives a title and the instruction that actually runs from the typed sentence, and that the item is only created when they send.
Says the result arrives in their notifications and that past attempts live in the item's run history — not in a chat thread, an email, or a colleague's screen.
ex-cowork-basics-life.guidance: Pass a plain, specific walkthrough even if the wording is informal. Do not pass an answer that only says "it runs automatically", that describes a back-and-forth conversation with follow-up questions, that sends the result to a colleague or an inbox, or that omits where the result is read. A wrong button choice (Schedule for work starting now, or the reverse) should fail the second criterion but need not sink the whole answer.

practiceTopic.title: Cowork basics
practiceTopic.summary: How a cowork item is created, what the chips decide, where its result is delivered, and who can see it.
facts: The Cowork row sits directly under New Chat in the sidebar, and its badge counts the items that are currently active.
The send button reads Run when the work starts now and Schedule when it starts later; while it is submitting it reads Starting…
A finished run is delivered to the notification centre under the Cowork category, and every attempt is listed in the item's What happened card.
A chip you set yourself — When, Repeat or Run as — always wins; Bee Flow only fills in the chips you left untouched.

Run as hands the brief to one of your agents, which brings its own skills, knowledge and connected apps; the result then also lands in that agent's chat thread, and the model tier is forced to Auto because the agent's own model runs it.
Apps it may use is a per-item allow-list: by default the item follows your workspace-wide list, and switching anything in the picker gives it its own list until you click Follow my workspace list.
Cowork items are personal: every read is scoped to the signed-in user, and there is no organisation-wide cowork list.
The cards above What happened read Runs, Succeeded and Average: Runs is the lifetime tally while individual run rows are kept for 90 days, and each person can keep 10 cowork items at a time.
